title: Instantaneous Velocity and Acceleration
notes: **Type 2 — alternate treatment:** this version complements the original note with the limit-definition approach, calculus forms and graphical slope reasoning for instantaneous velocity and acceleration.

**Average quantities first:** average velocity $v_{avg} = \frac{\Delta x}{\Delta t}$ uses the whole interval; average acceleration $a_{avg} = \frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t}$ likewise. They smooth out everything that happened in between — a car doing 100 km in 2 h has $v_{avg} = 50$ km/h regardless of traffic.

**The limit idea:** instantaneous velocity is the average velocity as $\Delta t \to 0$: $v = \lim_{\Delta t \to 0}\frac{\Delta x}{\Delta t} = \frac{dx}{dt}$. It answers 'how fast RIGHT NOW' — exactly what a speedometer reads.
**Instantaneous acceleration:** $a = \lim_{\Delta t \to 0}\frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t} = \frac{dv}{dt} = \frac{d^2x}{dt^2}$. Acceleration is the derivative of velocity — the 'slope of the slope'.

**Graphical meaning:** on an $x$–$t$ graph, velocity = slope of the tangent at the instant (not the chord); on a $v$–$t$ graph, acceleration = slope of the tangent, and the AREA under the curve between two times gives the displacement.

**Sign reasoning:** $v > 0$ → moving forward; $v < 0$ → moving backward; $a > 0$ with $v > 0$ → speeding up; $a > 0$ with $v < 0$ → slowing down (a negative velocity becoming more negative). 'Slowing down' means $v$ and $a$ have OPPOSITE signs — the classic exam trap.

**Worked calculus example:** $x(t) = 5t^2 - 3t$. Then $v = dx/dt = 10t - 3$ and $a = dv/dt = 10\,\text{m/s}^2$ (constant). At $t = 2$ s: $v = 17$ m/s; the particle is momentarily at rest when $t = 0.3$ s.

**Uniform vs non-uniform acceleration:** if $a$ is constant the SUVAT equations apply; if $a$ varies with time, position or velocity, only the calculus definitions (or graphs) work. This is why the derivative definition is the more general and more fundamental one.

**NEB exam focus:** define instantaneous velocity/acceleration as limits; differentiate a given $x(t)$; find when a particle is at rest or reverses; convert between $x$–$t$, $v$–$t$ and $a$–$t$ graphs (slopes and areas).
confusion: ❌ 'Instantaneous velocity equals average velocity.' ✅ Only when motion is uniform. In general $v_{inst} = dx/dt$ while $v_{avg} = \Delta x/\Delta t$; they coincide only if the $x$–$t$ graph is a straight line.

❌ 'Negative acceleration always means slowing down.' ✅ Slowing means $v$ and $a$ have OPPOSITE signs. A ball thrown upward (up = positive) has $v > 0$ with $a = -g$ — it slows going up and speeds up coming down, with the SAME downward acceleration throughout.
❌ 'The area under an $x$–$t$ graph gives velocity.' ✅ The SLOPE of $x$–$t$ gives velocity; the AREA under a $v$–$t$ graph gives displacement. Mixing these up is the classic graph-question error.
❌ 'At the turning point, acceleration is zero.' ✅ At a reversal, $v = 0$ but $a$ is NOT zero (e.g. a ball at the top of its flight has $v = 0$, $a = g$ downward). Zero velocity ≠ zero acceleration.
❌ 'Speed can be negative.' ✅ Speed is $|v|$, always non-negative; velocity carries the sign (direction).
❌ 'If $v = 0$ at an instant, the particle has stopped permanently.' ✅ $v = 0$ can be a momentary pause (top of a throw) — check the acceleration to know what happens next.
practice: Given $x(t) = 4t^3 - 2t^2 + 5$ (m): find $v(t)$ and $a(t)$; evaluate at $t = 1$ s. — $v = 12t^2 - 4t = 8$ m/s; $a = 24t - 4 = 20$ m/s².
A particle's velocity is $v(t) = 6t - 3t^2$ (m/s). When is it instantaneously at rest, and what is its acceleration then? — $t = 0$ or $2$ s; at $t = 2$: $a = 6 - 6t = -6$ m/s².
From a $v$–$t$ graph consisting of a straight line from (0, 4) to (4, 12) m/s, find the acceleration and the displacement in 4 s. — $a = 2$ m/s²; displacement = area $= \frac{4+12}{2}\times4 = 32$ m.
A stone is thrown up at 20 m/s ($g = 10$ m/s²). Find its velocity and acceleration at the highest point. — $v = 0$; $a = 10$ m/s² downward — zero velocity, non-zero acceleration.
The position of two trains is $x_1 = 20t$ and $x_2 = 5t^2$ (m). When are their instantaneous velocities equal, and where? — $20 = 10t$ → $t = 2$ s at $x = 40$ m.
universalFacts: Calculus was invented (Newton and Leibniz, 1660s–70s) precisely to handle instantaneous quantities — physics and calculus were born together, and Newton's name for the derivative was the 'fluxion'.
Car speedometers show instantaneous speed, while trip computers computing distance ÷ time show average speed — the two can differ enormously in city traffic.

Radar guns and GPS speed trackers estimate instantaneous velocity by measuring position over very small time windows — a physical implementation of the limit $\Delta x/\Delta t$ with $\Delta t \to 0$.
In relativity and quantum mechanics, instantaneous velocity remains fundamental: particle accelerators track beam particles through billions of instantaneous velocity updates per second.
examples: Example 1: $x(t) = 3t^2$ m → $v = 6t$ m/s; at $t = 2$ s the instantaneous velocity is 12 m/s, while the average velocity over 0–2 s is $\frac{12-0}{2} = 6$ m/s — different because the motion speeds up.
Example 2: A metro train's $v$–$t$ graph: trapezoid of acceleration, cruise, braking. Displacement = area of trapezoid; acceleration = slope in each segment.
Example 3: $v(t) = 8 - 4t$: the particle reverses at $t = 2$ s where $v = 0$ but $a = -4$ m/s² throughout — illustrating reversal with constant acceleration.
Example 4: Two instants with equal speeds but different velocities: $v = +10$ m/s at $t_1$ and $v = -10$ m/s at $t_2$ — same speed, opposite direction of motion.
Example 5: From $a = 6t$ and $v(0) = 2$ m/s: integrate to $v = 3t^2 + 2$ and, with $x(0) = 0$, $x = t^3 + 2t$ — showing how derivatives run downward ($x \to v \to a$) and integrals run upward.
practiceQuestions: Q1. Define instantaneous velocity with the limit definition and explain its graphical meaning on an $x$–$t$ graph.
Q2. Distinguish between average acceleration and instantaneous acceleration with one example each.
Q3. For $x(t) = 2t^3 - 9t^2 + 12t$ (m), find when the velocity is zero and classify each instant (pause vs reversal).
Q4. Sketch the $v$–$t$ graph for a ball thrown vertically upward and returning; mark where $v = 0$ and the sign of $a$ throughout.
Q5. A particle moves with $v = kt$ where $k = 2$ m/s². Find its instantaneous acceleration and displacement after 3 s from rest.
formulas: Displacement from velocity: $x_2 - x_1 = \int_{t_1}^{t_2} v\,dt$ (area under $v$–$t$ curve)
Rest condition: $v = \frac{dx}{dt} = 0$; reversal check: sign change of $v$ around that instant
keyPoints: Instantaneous velocity is the slope of the tangent of the $x$–$t$ graph; instantaneous acceleration is the slope of the $v$–$t$ graph.
Displacement is the area under the $v$–$t$ graph; change in velocity is the area under the $a$–$t$ graph.
$v = 0$ does not imply $a = 0$ — turning points have zero velocity but non-zero acceleration.
Speeding up ⟺ $v$ and $a$ share the same sign; slowing down ⟺ opposite signs.
Derivatives go down the chain $x \to v \to a$; integrals go up $a \to v \to x$, using initial conditions.
The limit definition is valid for ANY motion — SUVAT equations are special cases of constant acceleration only.
summary: Instantaneous velocity and acceleration are defined as limits: $v = dx/dt$ and $a = dv/dt = d^2x/dt^2$. Graphically, $v$ is the tangent slope of the $x$–$t$ curve and $a$ the tangent slope of the $v$–$t$ curve, while areas under $v$–$t$ and $a$–$t$ curves give displacement and velocity change. These definitions work for all motion — uniform or not — making them more fundamental than the constant-acceleration equations. Key exam skills: differentiating given $x(t)$, locating rest/reversal instants, and reading slopes and areas correctly with attention to signs.
specialNotes: Note 1: Carry units through calculus: if $x$ is in metres and $t$ in seconds, $v$ is m/s and $a$ is m/s² automatically.
Note 2: NEB graph questions award marks for BOTH slope reasoning and area reasoning — label which you used.
Note 3: When integrating acceleration, always determine integration constants from given initial conditions.
Note 4: In 'is the particle speeding up?' questions, compare signs of $v$ and $a$ at that instant — not the sign of $a$ alone.
importantStatements: Statement 1: Instantaneous velocity is the limit of average velocity as the time interval tends to zero: $v = dx/dt$.
Statement 2: Instantaneous acceleration is the derivative of velocity with respect to time: $a = dv/dt$.
Statement 3: On a position–time graph the slope of the tangent at any instant gives the instantaneous velocity at that instant.
Statement 4: The area under a velocity–time curve between two instants equals the displacement in that interval, regardless of whether the acceleration is constant.
importantNotes: Note 1: Zero instantaneous velocity does not imply zero acceleration (turning points).
Note 2: Instantaneous speed equals the magnitude of instantaneous velocity, but never carries a direction.
Note 3: For constant acceleration only, $v_{avg} = (u+v)/2$; this shortcut fails when $a$ varies.
Note 4: The calculus definitions apply to ALL motion; SUVAT equations are the special case of constant $a$.
examShortTricks: Trick 1: 'At rest' ⇒ set $dx/dt = 0$ and solve for $t$; then check the sign of $v$ on both sides to classify pause vs reversal.
Trick 2: In graph MCQs, remember: slope of $x$–$t$ = $v$; slope of $v$–$t$ = $a$; area of $v$–$t$ = $x$; area of $a$–$t$ = $v$.
Trick 3: If $x(t)$ is a polynomial, differentiate term-by-term ($d(t^n)/dt = nt^{n-1}$) — no formula sheet needed.
Trick 4: 'Maximum/minimum position' questions ⇒ set $v = dx/dt = 0$, exactly like turning points in calculus.
Trick 5: Units self-check: differentiate $x$ in metres → $v$ in m/s → $a$ in m/s²; if your units don't cascade, recheck the algebra.
examNotes: Exam Tip 1: NEB regularly sets 2-3 mark calculus questions: differentiate $x(t)$, evaluate $v$ and $a$ at a given time — show the derivative step explicitly.
Exam Tip 2: In graph-conversion questions (given $v$–$t$, sketch $x$–$t$), track curvature: constant $v$ → straight $x$ line; linear $v$ → parabolic $x$.
Exam Tip 3: When asked 'when is the particle at rest', also state the acceleration at that instant — examiners expect the follow-through.
Exam Tip 4: Define the limit properly in theory questions: shrinking interval, ratio of small changes — vague wording loses marks.

importantConcepts: Concept 1: Limit definition — instantaneous quantities are average quantities over a vanishing interval.
Concept 2: Derivative chain: $x \xrightarrow{d/dt} v \xrightarrow{d/dt} a$; integrals run the reverse way with initial conditions.
Concept 3: Graph duality — slopes give rates (v, a); areas give accumulations (x, v).
Concept 4: Sign logic — direction of motion from sign of $v$; speeding up/slowing down from relative signs of $v$ and $a$.
Concept 5: Generality — the derivative definitions hold for any acceleration; constant-$a$ equations are a special case.
